analysis.evidence: In לָמָּה חָרָה לָךְ, Yahweh asks Cain why he is angry. The parallel question וְלָמָּה נָפְלוּ פָנֶיךָ likewise asks the reason for his downcast expression.
analysis.morphology: Interrogative pronoun מָה with the prefixed preposition לְ, forming the interrogative adverb לָמָּה.
analysis.sense: Asks the reason for a state or action.

analysis.evidence: In לָמָּה חָרָה לָךְ, the verb is impersonal. לָךְ identifies Cain as the one who feels the anger, yielding ‘Why have you become angry?’ The parallel question asks why his face has fallen.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular

draft.change: Add Gen.4.6 as an example of the existing Hebrew ‘why?’ sense.
draft.definition: With לְ, מָה asks why something is so or why it happened.
draft.evidence: In Gen.4.6 Yahweh asks Cain why his face has fallen.

analysis.evidence: In וְלָמָּה נָפְלוּ פָנֶיךָ, ‘and why has your face fallen?’, וְ joins this question to Yahweh’s preceding question about Cain’s anger. The repeated לָמָּה asks Cain to account for his fallen expression.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וְ ‘and’ + preposition לְ ‘for’ + interrogative pronoun מָה ‘what’. Together לָמָּה functions adverbially as ‘why’.
analysis.sense: With לְ, asks for the reason for a state or event.

analysis.evidence: נָפְלוּ agrees with the plural subject פָנֶיךָ, “your face.” The question “Why has your face fallen?” describes Cain’s downcast expression alongside the preceding question about his anger.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person common plural

analysis.evidence: In וְלָמָּה נָפְלוּ פָנֶיךָ, “and why has your face fallen?”, the plural verb נָפְלוּ agrees with פָנֶיךָ. The suffix addresses Cain, and the parallel question about his anger identifies his fallen face as a visible expression of his mood.
analysis.morphology: Common noun of both genders, plural construct with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix.
